docs.title: ABCD Biopsychosocial Prediction
docs.text:
High-dimensional ensemble stacking machine learning pipeline for hierarchical, interactive, and dynamic prediction of psychiatric, cognitive, and social outcomes in the ABCD Study.

Which of the wide range of currently available biopsychosocial measurements best predict hallmark psychiatric outcomes in adolescents and adults, and where do they converge or diverge in their predictive architecture? This is the code behind Roberts et al., Psychiatry and Its Hierarchical & Dynamic Discontents: Biopsychosocial Prediction in Depression, Anxiety, ADHD, Social Relationships, and Cognition (under review at Nature).

Fig 5 of the article: within-category ensemble meta-model performance (R²) for adolescent anxiety and hallmark low-mood/depression features in each biopsychosocial measurement category, at every available wave from age 9 to 13. Feature sets from age 9 were also used to predict age 13 outcomes.

Fig 7 of the article: across-category ensemble performance and the top 15 consensus-weighted features for five adult targets at baseline, 2-year and 4-year follow-up. Ribbon width and opacity reflect weighted ensemble importance, and shared features are annotated (nT).

docs.title: Checking the article's code
docs.text: The exact code used for the article is the notebook in paper/ (release v1.0.0, Zenodo). Methods in brief describes what it does, Reproducing the paper maps each figure and supplementary analysis to its stages and settings, and Equivalence shows that this package gives the same results as the notebook at every stage on simulated panels.

docs.title: Running it on ABCD data
docs.text: Read Data access and governance, then Installation, Reproducing the paper and Configuration.

docs.title: Trying it without ABCD data
docs.text:
Follow the Quickstart. It runs in a minute or two on a laptop and checks that the pipeline recovers a planted signal.

pip install -e .
bpsp example-panel outputs/example_panel.csv
bpsp run configs/demo.yaml

docs.title: Simulated example data
docs.text:
Simulated panels with a known answer, for demonstrations and tests.

The panel shipped in data/simulated/ draws every column independently, so no outcome can be predicted from it. :func:make_example_panel resamples it to a chosen number of subjects and plants a known structure at wave T2 (time == 2), so that a run has a correct answer to recover:

  • a latent score drives three parent-report CBCL items (stubborn_p, disagreeable_p, blames_others_p, recorded as 0/1/2);
  • the CBCL internalizing and depression T-scores (internal_D_p, depress_D_p) are 55 + 6 * (0.8 * latent + 0.6 * delta_not_liked_p + noise), and the externalizing score (external_D_p) uses 0.7 times the same signal;
  • the binary depression targets of the "Child Depression Worsening" batch (top_10_depression, top_5_depression, dep_increase_1.5sd, dep_increase_2sd) are thresholds of that signal;
  • the noise standard deviation is 1.3 instead of 0.8 for participants with desc_latin_B == 1, so the subgroup analyses have a real difference to detect.

Everything else carries no information, and baseline demographics are held constant within subject. The data remain fully synthetic.

docs.title: From notebook to package
docs.text:
The pipeline was written and used for the paper as a 25-cell Colab notebook (about 38,000 lines), frozen as release v1.0.0 in paper/. Version 2 turns it into an installable package with the same results, apart from the few deliberate changes listed in Equivalence.

Results of the published notebook were recorded on a simulated panel before anything changed, and every step of the conversion was checked against them. Notebook cells became modules, Colab form fields became typed configuration, and the global namespace the cells shared became one explicit run context.

The conversion itself was done with a syntax-tree codemod (libcst) that keeps the code as written, so each module still reads like its notebook cell. Formatting (ruff), the switch from print to logging and the later tidying of comments were each checked to leave every module's syntax tree unchanged apart from the logging calls. The conversion tooling was used once and is not part of this repository. From v2.0.0 on, the package is the source and is edited directly.

flowchart LR
    CFG[PipelineConfig<br/>YAML] --> P[Pipeline]
    P --> S[setup<br/>registry · circularity · spectrum · preprocessing · stacking]
    S --> M[main<br/>stacking ensemble per target]
    M --> R[reports<br/>batch summary · Sankey]
    M --> I[interpretation<br/>networks · diagnostics]
    M --> V[validation suite<br/>13 analyses + smoke test]
    CTX[(RunContext ctx)] -.shared state.- S
    CTX -.- M
    CTX -.- R
    CTX -.- I
    CTX -.- V

docs.title: The run context
docs.text:
In the notebook every cell read and wrote one global namespace: the main runner left X_train, metrics_dict_full or _batch_archive behind, and validation cells picked them up. In the package that namespace is a single object, bpsp.ctx (a RunContext, which is a dict with attribute access):

  • stage settings are written into it before each stage runs, exactly when the notebook cell would have set its form fields
  • stages read their inputs from it and write their outputs to it, so ctx.X_train or ctx.metrics_dict_full can be inspected after any stage
  • Pipeline.setup() resets it, so every session starts clean

Shared names are written as ctx.<name> in the code, so every cross-stage dependency is visible with a text search, and each stage's inputs and outputs are listed in Stage data flow below.

Rewriting every function to take its inputs as arguments would have meant re-deriving the behavior of 38,000 lines by hand. The run context gives the same visibility while keeping the verified behavior. With the equivalence tests in place, individual stages can now be refactored into pure functions one at a time.

The stacking model keeps one more notebook pattern. StackingEnsembleModel gets its final fit, predict and predict_proba methods from enhance_stacking_ensemble_model() in bpsp.models.stacking, which v1.0.0 used to add the interaction meta-features (pairwise products and mean) to the class after defining it. It is kept as written so that the fitted models stay identical.

docs.title: Code quality
docs.text: The hand-written modules (pipeline, config, context, cli, _logging, simulation) are fully type-annotated and checked with mypy, and have 94% unit-test coverage. The stage modules keep the notebook's code and style and are checked by the integration and equivalence tests, and by ruff with a few rules relaxed for them (listed in pyproject.toml).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Each notebook form field became a typed field of a stage dataclass in bpsp.config, with the published value as default and the notebook's drop-down options as allowed values. PipelineConfig combines them with the list of stages, the output directory and optional model hyperparameter overrides, and reads and writes YAML. Invalid stage names, unknown settings and out-of-range choices fail fast with a clear message.

docs.title: Logging and outputs
docs.text: Stage output goes through the bpsp logger. The default console handler prints messages unformatted to the current sys.stdout, which reproduces the notebook's printed output in Jupyter and in a terminal. Styled tables and HTML notes are shown with IPython's display, so they render in Jupyter and Colab. bpsp run prints them as plain text instead. The command line also saves everything the console shows to run.log, plus the resolved configuration, next to the tables and figures in the output directory.

docs.title: Optional dependencies
docs.text: TabPFN and PyTorch are an optional extra. Without them the package runs on CPU and TabPFN is left out of the ensemble, as the notebook already did for across-category runs.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Changes are documented here. The project follows Semantic Versioning.

Version 2 changes transformed notebook into an installable & tested Python package. On the equivalence runs described in docs/equivalence.md it gives the same results as v1.0.0, apart from the deliberate changes listed under Changed.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• bpsp package (src/bpsp/): one module per notebook cell, grouped into data, models, analysis, reports, interpretation and validation.
  • Pipeline orchestration with setup, ordered stages, per-stage timings and an output directory per run.
  • Typed configuration (PipelineConfig) for every former Colab form field, with the notebook's values as defaults. Drop-down choices and types are validated on load, misspelled settings are rejected, and configurations are read and written as YAML.
  • Command-line interface: bpsp run, bpsp stages, bpsp init-config, bpsp example-panel.
  • Explicit run context (bpsp.ctx) for state shared between stages.
  • Logging through the bpsp logger. bpsp run prints tables as text and saves the console output (run.log) and the resolved configuration with each run.
  • Tests: unit, end-to-end on simulated data, known-answer, and equivalence with the published notebook. GitHub Actions CI with ruff, mypy, coverage and actionlint.
  • Documentation site, including Concepts and Methods in brief pages, a model card, a data governance guide, a contribution guide and a citation file.
  • Data-protection guards: .gitignore rules, a pre-commit hook and a CI check that block data, statistics-package and archive files, large files and ABCD participant identifiers.
  • Optional tabpfn extra. CPU-only installs leave TabPFN out of the ensemble and the stacking audit automatically.
  • setup.objective_subjective_spectrum switch for the objective/subjective gradient (notebook cell 3).
  • bpsp.simulation: a simulated panel with a known signal, used by the demo, the quickstart notebook and the known-answer tests.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The main stage takes its CatBoost settings from PIPELINE_MODEL_CONFIGS, so model_overrides reach it. v1.0.0 kept a second copy of the same values in the runner. Defaults are unchanged.
  • The main stage reads the ensemble's metrics from meta_model directly. v1.0.0 first looked up an entry that never exists and printed [WARNING] 'ensemble' on every run.
  • Messages and figure titles name stages and settings instead of notebook cells, the Colab form or review points ([POINT 1] became [nested_cv]), and no longer say "Enhanced". The permutation report is titled after the CatBoost model it tests. A development note printed by the networks stage was removed.
  • Comments and docstrings were tidied, and docstrings that described the permutation test as refitting the stacking ensemble were corrected.
  • Each session works on its own copies of the variable registry, so runs in one process do not affect each other.
  • All tables and figures are written to the configured output directory.
  • CatBoostPruningCallback is imported from optuna_integration (the same class). The optuna.integration path is deprecated and will be removed in Optuna 6.
  • Printed output goes through logging, with the same text on the console.
  • The versions v1.0.0 was tested with moved from requirements.txt to paper/requirements.txt, next to the v1.0.0 notebook. requirements-lock.txt pins the environment in which v2.0.0 was verified.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The terms used across the pipeline, the article and these pages.

docs.title: Waves (T0 to T4)
docs.text: The five annual ABCD assessment waves used here. T0 is baseline (ages 9 to 10) and T4 is the fourth annual follow-up (ages 13 to 14). The setting main.tp_option picks the wave of the target. Parent self-report (ASR) was only collected at T0, T2 and T4, two years apart, while parent ratings of the child (CBCL) were collected at every wave.

docs.title: Measurement categories
docs.text: Variables were feature-engineered into theoretically relevant, commonly used, or potentially informative measurement categories (domains), such as Other Personality Features, Family Dynamics & Parenting, Technology Use or Structural and DTI. The variable registry (bpsp.data.registry) holds 37 adolescent and 32 parent categories across the five waves, 27 and 22 of them at baseline, because some categories only exist at some waves. Figure 1 of the article shows the 30 primary adolescent and 20 parent categories. The registry lists every category and its variables per wave (CHILD_VARIABLES_BY_TIMEPOINT, PARENT_VARIABLES_BY_TIMEPOINT).

docs.title: Variable names and figure labels
docs.text: The analysis panel uses interpretable variable names. data/variable_map.csv gives each one's source ABCD table and original variable name (derived composites, change scores and thresholds are marked derived) and its figure label. For accessibility, a display-name dictionary translating coded variables into natural-language labels is applied to the feature-importance outputs and figures (DISPLAY_NAMES and TARGET_DISPLAY_NAMES in bpsp.data.preprocessing).

docs.title: Within-category and across-category models
docs.text: Within-category models fit one stacking ensemble per measurement category, so categories can be compared with each other (Figs 3, 5 and 6). Across-category models use all non-circular measures together, to find the most predictive features and interactions across categories (Figs 7 and 8, Fex1 and Fex2). The setting is main.split (within_categories or across_categories).

docs.title: Circularity exclusions
docs.text: For every target, a structured protocol removes predictors on three criteria: variables already subsumed in the target (for example the CBCL sadness item when predicting depression), predictors with theoretical or ontological overlap with the target that raters could plausibly conflate with it, and likely or ambiguous reverse-causation confounds. Within-category models drop specific features and sometimes whole categories. Across-category models drop features per target. The lists are in bpsp.data.circularity. The protocol reduces direct leakage but does not eliminate all rater, method, or ambiguous latent construct covariance.

docs.title: Concurrent and prospective prediction
docs.text: Concurrent prediction uses features from the same wave as the target. Prospective prediction uses features from an earlier wave, for example baseline features (age ~9) predicting outcomes at age 11 (2-year) or age 13 (4-year). The setting is main.feature_tp_option: Match target for concurrent prediction, or an earlier wave.

docs.title: Trait-like and change-based predictors
docs.text: Trait-like predictors are dispositional characteristics such as personality or cognitive style. Change-based (delta) predictors are changes since the previous wave, computed for theoretically important measures when the previous wave was available (for example other psychopathology, social problems, family conflict, adverse life events and school problems). Delta variables start with delta_.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text: The article's Methods pre-specify the primary outcomes as adolescent depression (syndrome and primary-feature composites), anxiety, ADHD and social problems, and parent depression (ASR syndrome and single-item self-reported depressed mood). Other targets, such as externalizing, cognitive and academic outcomes, depression subtypes, happiness and relationship problems, are exploratory contrasts. Core depression targets leave out the secondary features of sleep, appetite and self-harm to focus on the hallmark features of low mood. The higher-order internalizing and externalizing spectra are the CBCL (adolescents) and ASR (parents) broadband scales. In the configuration, the bundles named Child P-Factor and Parent P-Factor hold these spectra and keep their v1.0.0 names.

docs.title: Objective/subjective gradient
docs.text: An alternative parcellation of the same variables along a seven-level objective-to-subjective gradient, separating child and parent report, from Objective No-Report measures (neuroimaging, experimental tasks, physical measurements, genetic ancestry components) to parent self-report and parent-reported family measures (Fig 4). It is turned on with setup.objective_subjective_spectrum.

docs.title: Stacking ensemble
docs.text: CatBoost, XGBoost, random forest and, in within-category models, TabPFN are the base learners. Each produces out-of-fold predictions on the training data, and a meta-learner (linear regression for continuous targets, logistic regression for binary ones) combines them. See Methods in brief.

docs.title: Consensus importance
docs.text: Each base learner's feature importance, normalized to its largest value, multiplied by that learner's contribution to the meta-learner and summed across learners. In within-category models TabPFN does not contribute to it (see Methods in brief). Because tree-based and SHAP importance can split credit among correlated predictors, importance within highly correlated feature clusters is best read at the cluster level (the grouped_importance stage, Supplement S5.4).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A run is configured by one YAML file (or a PipelineConfig object). Every key is optional; missing keys keep the published defaults. bpsp init-config FILE writes a file with every setting.

stages: [main, nested_cv]          # stages to run after setup, in order
output_dir: outputs/my_run         # tables, figures, run.log, config.resolved.yaml
model_overrides:                   # optional hyperparameter overrides per base learner
  catboost: {iterations: 300}
setup:
  DATA_PATH: /secure/abcd/CLEAN_ABCD_5.1_panel.csv
main:
  target_options: depress_D_p
  split: within_categories
nested_cv:
  n_outer_folds: 10

Setting names are identical to the form fields of the published notebook, so each one can be traced to the paper version. Settings with a fixed set of values are validated when the configuration is loaded.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thanks for your interest. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

docs.title: Ground rules for data
docs.text:
• Never commit ABCD data or anything derived from it at participant level (predictions, residuals, row-level tables), and never paste such data into issues. Use the simulated panel in data/simulated/ to reproduce problems.
  • Keep real-data runs outside the repository folder.
  • The pre-commit hook and CI block data files and ABCD participant identifiers. Do not bypass them.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pre-commit install

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
ruff check . && ruff format --check .
mypy                                         # the hand-written modules
pytest -m "not integration and not slow"   # unit tests, seconds
pytest -m integration                        # end-to-end on the simulated panel, a few minutes
pytest -m slow                               # equivalence with the published notebook, under an hour

make help lists shortcuts for the same checks and for the demo, the notebook and the docs.

docs.title: Changing analysis code
docs.text:
The stage modules are a faithful port of the published notebook, and the equivalence test (tests/regression/) checks that they still reproduce it. When a change is meant to keep results identical, run pytest -m slow before opening a pull request. When a change is meant to alter results (a bug fix, a new method), say so in the pull request and in CHANGELOG.md, explain the effect on the simulated panel, and add the change to the documented edits in tests/regression/equivalence.py.

Style: ruff (configured in pyproject.toml), NumPy-style docstrings for public functions, type hints checked by mypy for the hand-written modules, and logger instead of print.

After changing configuration fields or what a stage reads and writes, regenerate the reference pages with python tools/gen_docs.py (CI checks that they are current).

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
1. Update src/bpsp/_version.py, CHANGELOG.md and the version and date-released fields of CITATION.cff (semantic versioning).
  2. Tag vX.Y.Z on main and publish a GitHub release with the changelog entry.
  3. Archive the release on Zenodo with New version on the existing record, so all versions share one concept DOI.

The tag v1.0.0 and paper/ always hold the exact code used for the article.

docs.title: ABCD data
docs.text:
The analyses use the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, Release 5.1: N = 11,864 adolescents (ages 9 to 14) and N ≈ 11,859 parents or caregivers, across five annual waves (T0 to T4).

ABCD data can only be used under an approved Data Use Certification (DUC). The article used Release 5.1, obtained through the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). The NDA no longer accepts new ABCD access requests: access now goes through the NIH Brain Development Cohorts (NBDC) Data Hub, which also hosts later releases. The variable registry uses Release 5.1 variable names.

This repository contains no ABCD data and must never contain any, including participant-level outputs (predictions, residuals, row-level tables) produced from ABCD data. The ABCD terms also prohibit putting ABCD data into generative AI tools.

docs.title: What is in the repository
docs.text: File Contents data/simulated/CLEAN_ABCD_5_1_panel_simulated.csv Fully simulated panel: same columns and five-wave structure as the analysis file, values drawn at random from column-level summaries. No participant data, no real associations. data/variable_map.csv Each variable in the analysis file with its source ABCD table, original variable name and figure label: the dictionary the article provides with the code and in Supplement S1.1. Derived composites, change scores and thresholds are marked derived.

docs.title: Safeguards
docs.text:
• .gitignore excludes common tabular, statistics-package (SPSS, Stata, SAS, R), array and archive formats, except the two files above.
  • A pre-commit hook (tools/check_no_participant_data.py) blocks the same file types, any other file over 5 MB, and any file containing ABCD participant identifiers (NDAR_INV...). CI runs the same check on every pull request and every push to main. Archives are blocked because their contents cannot be checked.
  • Run outputs go to outputs/ by default, which is ignored by git, as are figures (PNG, PDF, SVG). Keep real-data outputs outside the repository folder altogether.

If ABCD data or participant-level outputs are ever committed by mistake, deleting them in a new commit is not enough: the history must be rewritten (for example with git filter-repo), forks checked, and GitHub Support asked to purge cached views. Check your DUC for reporting obligations.

docs.title: Expected input format
docs.text:
• One row per participant per wave, with subject and time (0 to 4) columns.
  • Feature columns named as in data/variable_map.csv, with target variables, change scores and neuroimaging components already computed.
  • Family ID (rel_family_id) and site ID (L_site_id) columns for grouped cross-validation.

The merged file is built with the extraction code in the companion repository abcd-visualizations-and-data.

docs.title: Equivalence with v1.0.0
docs.text: Version 2.0.0 restructures the published notebook into a package. It does not re-implement it. This page records how that was checked and what the checks found.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Both versions were run on the same data with the same settings and compared after every step.

The data were panels of simulated subjects over five waves, resampled from the fully simulated panel in data/simulated/, with a planted signal so that the models learn something and any difference in the code path shows up in the numbers. The four test plans in tests/regression/plans/ use 400 subjects. No ABCD data were used.

v1.0.0 is paper/ABCDMLPipeline_v1.0.0.ipynb, executed cell by cell in one IPython namespace, as Colab runs it, with the form fields set to the values of the run plan before each cell. v2.0.0 runs the same plan through bpsp.Pipeline, stage by stage.

Both runs use the same seeds (the pipeline's own), PYTHONHASHSEED=0 (set by the test harness) and the CPU only, with smaller base learners and fewer resamples so that a run takes minutes rather than days. TabPFN and PyTorch are not installed in the test environment, so on both sides TabPFN is replaced by a small linear stand-in (tests/regression/stubs/), which only the within-category plan fits. The test plans also seed Python's and NumPy's global random generators identically before every step, because two v1.0.0 figures draw from them unseeded: ncv_fold_dist.png (random jitter of the outer-fold points) and stratified_feature_importance.png (Kernel SHAP sampling). Without that seeding these two figures change from run to run in v1.0.0 itself, while the tables behind them stay the same.

After each step three things are compared:

  1. Shared results. Every object that later stages read (train and test matrices and targets, metrics, batch archives, consensus importance, ensemble weights, validation tables) is fingerprinted: arrays and data frames are hashed after rounding to six decimals, and scalars are compared with a relative tolerance of 10-6.
  2. Printed output. The full text output of each analysis stage, line by line. Left out are stage start and end lines, lines that contain "Warning" or come from Python's warnings (including the pipeline's own warning messages), traceback layout (the error itself is compared), progress bars, blank lines and IPython's echo of a cell's value. Setup output is not compared, because importing the modules prints the same lines as notebook cells 0 to 5 in a different order.
  3. Files. Every table and figure written: CSV files by value, PNG files byte for byte, PDF files byte for byte apart from their embedded creation date.

The deliberate changes listed below are applied to v1.0.0 before the comparison, exactly as listed in tests/regression/equivalence.py. Nothing else is edited.

docs.title: Deliberate source changes
docs.text:
These changes were made on purpose and each is covered by the runs above. The first seven leave every result and printed line as it was. The last four change printed text, figure titles or values in some cases, so the equivalence harness applies them to v1.0.0 before comparing (V1_SOURCE_EDITS, V1_TEXT_EDITS, V2_MESSAGE_EDITS and V2_DROPPED_LINES in tests/regression/equivalence.py).

Change Why Each session works on copies of the variable registry The optional objective/subjective gradient edits the registry in place. Copies keep sessions in one process independent. TabPFN and PyTorch imports are optional CPU-only installs work. Without them TabPFN is skipped and the reason logged, as the notebook already did for across-category runs, and the stacking audit checks the other base learners. print became logging through the bpsp logger The console shows the same text, and run.log keeps it. Checked by comparing syntax trees (identical apart from the logging calls) and by the printed-output comparison. Imports inside a stage's main code are declared global In the notebook they bound globals. Inside a function they would otherwise shadow the module-level import on paths where they do not run. CatBoostPruningCallback imported from optuna_integration instead of optuna.integration It is the same class. The old path is deprecated and will be removed in Optuna 6. Box-drawing characters in two f-strings written literally Python 3.11 does not accept backslash escapes inside f-string expressions. The printed text is identical. Comments and docstrings tidied, a block of commented-out code removed, and the private _run_val_NN helpers renamed _run_for_current_target Readability. A syntax-tree comparison that ignores docstrings shows no other change. The main stage takes its CatBoost settings from PIPELINE_MODEL_CONFIGS v1.0.0 kept a second copy of the same values in the main runner, so changing the central dictionary did not reach the main stage. The defaults are identical, so results only change when settings are overridden (model_overrides). The main stage reads the ensemble's metrics from meta_model directly v1.0.0 first looked up an ensemble entry the metrics never contain, printed [WARNING] 'ensemble' on every run and then used meta_model. The numbers are the same and the misleading line is gone. Adjusted R² is reported as missing (NaN) when the test rows do not exceed the number of predictors plus one The formula is undefined there, and v1.0.0 printed values above 1. This happens on small panels like the demo's. At the article's sample sizes the values are unchanged. Messages and figure titles name stages and settings instead of notebook cells, the Colab form or review points ([POINT 1] became [nested_cv]), "Enhanced" was dropped from messages, the permutation report is titled after the CatBoost model it tests, and the networks stage no longer prints a development note about a target-inclusive network that v1.0.0 does not implement A package has stages, not cells or review points.

docs.title: What the conversion found
docs.text:
Converting the notebook surfaced issues that v1.0.0 has as well. They are kept as they are, so that the two versions agree, and are listed in Known issues:

  • 15 names are referenced but never defined in v1.0.0, and one is used before it is assigned in its function, all in rarely used branches
  • three label dictionaries repeat keys (the later label is used)
  • two figures use unseeded random numbers, and the fairness forest plot fails when confidence limits cannot be computed
  • TabPFN does not contribute to the consensus importance of within-category models

docs.text:

pytest -m slow    # four smaller runs on a 400-subject panel

or step by step with tests/regression/equivalence.py (panel, notebook, package, compare). The equivalence workflow on GitHub Actions runs the same tests weekly.

docs.text:

  • At least 16 GB of system RAM for across-category feature combinations (32 GB recommended for full within-category sweeps across all waves).
  • v1.0.0 was run on Ubuntu 22.04 (Colab), macOS 14 and Windows 11 via WSL2. v2.0.0 is tested on Linux in CI.

docs.title: Known issues inherited from v1.0.0
docs.text:

docs.title: Other findings kept as written
docs.text:
Three label dictionaries repeat keys: delta_not_liked_p in DISPLAY_NAMES, anhedonia_B_k and depressed_mood_B_k in TARGET_DISPLAY_NAMES, and suicidal_p in _BATCH_TARGET_COLORS. As in v1.0.0 the later entry is used, which only affects figure labels and colors.

Comparisons such as df["high_ale"] == True are element-wise pandas operations and are correct as written. The corresponding lint rule is switched off for the stage modules.

Two figures draw from NumPy's global random generator, which v1.0.0 never seeds: the horizontal jitter of the outer-fold points in ncv_fold_dist.png (nested CV) and the Kernel SHAP sampling behind stratified_feature_importance.png (stratified stage, when no tree explainer applies). They differ slightly from run to run. The tables behind them matched exactly in the equivalence runs.

The diagnostics stage's effect-size and cross-validation versus held-out comparisons stop with a feature-count mismatch (for example 550 versus 519 features). They score the last fitted model on the run context's test matrix as it was before the main stage's own preprocessing (categorical encoding and removal of constant and duplicate columns). The stage logs the error and continues.

The fairness stage's forest plot raises ValueError: Axis limits cannot be NaN or Inf when no confidence limits can be computed for a target, which happens when groups are very small (seen on the 400-subject test panel). The stage then stops at that target, and later stages are unaffected.

When a within-category feature set has more than 100 features, the CatBoost screen that picks TabPFN's 100 features is fitted on the whole training partition before the internal five-fold split. TabPFN's out-of-fold predictions, and so the meta-learner's inputs, have therefore seen that screening. The held-out test estimates are not affected.

In within-category models, TabPFN does not contribute to the consensus importance. The consensus step has no importance method for it, logs "Successfully calculated importance for tabpfn", then fails on that model and logs "Could not calculate importance for tabpfn". The consensus therefore comes from CatBoost, XGBoost and random forest, and TabPFN's share of the meta-learner weight is left out rather than redistributed. TabPFN's permutation importance is computed separately (get_feature_importance).

Outlier clipping (at five standard deviations from the mean) uses statistics computed within each set: the training rows for the training set and the test rows for the test set. No outcome information is involved, but the test set's bounds come from the test rows themselves. Imputation and scaling are fitted on the training rows only.

Messages are kept as v1.0.0 printed them, apart from the documented edits, so that the two versions can be compared line by line. A few overstate what runs, such as "Successfully calculated importance for tabpfn" above.

docs.title: Methods in brief
docs.text: What the pipeline does, following the Methods of the article. Terms are explained in Concepts, the settings in Configuration, and the article's REFORMS-ML checklist is in Supplement S1.1.

docs.title: Features and targets
docs.text:
About 1,078 unique variables were selected or created from 69 ABCD scales on three criteria: potential theoretical relevance to psychopathology, being most informative for comparing hierarchical differences and informing later research, and prior empirical evidence of association. They are organized into measurement categories per wave, with change-based (delta) variables where the previous wave was available. Each target gets its own circularity exclusions before any model is fitted.

Neuroimaging features were prepared in the analysis dataset before this pipeline runs: per modality, columns and rows with more than 20% missing data were dropped, remaining gaps imputed with MICE, and the data reduced to 75 principal components. That preparation used the whole sample, not only the training rows. Genetic ancestry components were previously derived from the ABCD genetic data with PC-AiR (Fan et al., 2023).

Inside the pipeline, for each target and wave:

  1. Variables with more than 70% missing values are dropped.
  2. The rows are split 70/30 into training and test sets.
  3. Missing feature values are imputed by k-nearest neighbors (k = 5), fitted on the training rows.
  4. Constant features are removed, and numeric features are clipped at five standard deviations from their mean. The mean and standard deviation are computed within the training rows for the training set and within the test rows for the test set.
  5. Features are standardized with a scaler fitted on the training rows.

docs.title: Stacking ensemble
docs.text:
Base learner Settings (fixed a priori) Used in CatBoost 1,000 iterations, learning rate 0.05, depth 6, l2_leaf_reg 3, border_count 128 all models XGBoost 500 estimators, learning rate 0.1, maximum depth 6, min_child_weight 1, subsample 0.8, colsample_bytree 0.8 all models Random forest 200 estimators, maximum depth 10 (for regression also min_samples_split 5, min_samples_leaf 2) all models TabPFN v2 its own defaults within-category models

For classification, CatBoost and random forest use balanced class weights, and for binary targets XGBoost's scale_pos_weight is the square root of the ratio of negative to positive cases. The main settings live in one dictionary, PIPELINE_MODEL_CONFIGS in bpsp.models.stacking, and a run can override them with model_overrides. The remaining settings above are fixed in StackingEnsembleModel. TabPFN is left out of across-category models because of its known instability above ~500 features, little added performance at that scale and high computational cost. When a within-category feature set has more than 100 features, TabPFN gets the 100 ranked highest by a small CatBoost model (100 iterations) fitted on the training partition.

Each base learner produces out-of-fold predictions on the training partition through an internal five-fold split. The meta-learner, linear regression for continuous targets and logistic regression for binary targets, is fitted on those out-of-fold predictions, their pairwise products and their mean. For classification its regularization strength is chosen by five-fold cross-validation within the training data. No other hyperparameters are tuned. The base learners are then refit on the full training partition. A global random seed (42) is used throughout, with shuffled splits (stratified for classification).

An optional hyperparameter search from the notebook (main.hyperparameter_tuning, which for the stacking ensemble searches CatBoost settings with Optuna when main.with_optuna is also on) is off by default and was not used for the article.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Primary estimates come from a 70/30 train/test split, stratified for classification targets. The held-out 30% is not used to fit any model. Regression is scored with R², adjusted R², MAE and RMSE, and classification with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, plus thresholds and calibration in the validation stages.

Adjusted R² applies the usual penalty for the number of candidate predictors to the held-out R², so it is a conservative reference value. It is undefined when the test rows do not exceed the number of predictors plus one, and is then reported as missing.

docs.title: Feature importance
docs.text: Consensus importance is each base learner's feature importance, scaled to its largest value, multiplied by that learner's weight in the meta-learner and summed across learners. A learner's weight is the absolute meta-learner coefficient on its out-of-fold prediction, as a share of the total over learners. In within-category models TabPFN does not contribute: the consensus step computes no importance for it, so the consensus comes from CatBoost, XGBoost and random forest with their meta-learner weights (Known issues). SHAP values are computed as well. Because tree-based and SHAP importance can split credit among correlated predictors, importance within highly correlated clusters should be read at the cluster level (networks for correlations among top features, ablation for domain permutation importance and top-K ablation, grouped_importance for grouped permutation importance).

docs.title: Model details
docs.text:
A two-stage stacking ensemble. The base learners are CatBoost, XGBoost, random forest and TabPFN (TabPFN only in within-category models). The meta-learner is linear regression for continuous targets and logistic regression for binary targets, fitted on the base learners' out-of-fold predictions, their pairwise products and their mean. Details are in Methods in brief.

Field Details Contributors Clark Roberts (conceptualization, feature-engineering, ML pipeline programming, implementation of manuscript models, statistical analysis, visualization), Zhafira E. Fawnia (Ensemble ML programming) Versions v1.0.0, the notebook used for the article; v2.0.0, this package, with the same results on simulated panels (Equivalence) License MIT for the code. ABCD data are governed by the ABCD Data Use Certification.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text:
Research on the comparative predictive utility of biological, psychological, social and environmental measurement domains for psychiatric, cognitive and social outcomes, at the population level.

The models are not meant for clinical decisions, diagnosis, screening or individual risk prediction. They were fitted and evaluated in a research cohort and have not been validated for any clinical population or setting.

docs.title: Training data
docs.text: ABCD Study Release 5.1, five annual waves (T0 to T4): 11,864 adolescents aged 9 to 14 and about 11,859 parents and caregivers aged 23 to 75. About 1,078 variables from 69 scales, organized into 37 adolescent and 32 parent measurement categories across the waves. Imputation and scaling inside the pipeline are fitted on training rows only. Neuroimaging components were computed in the analysis dataset beforehand, on the whole sample (Methods in brief).

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Primary estimates come from a held-out 30% test split. Nested cross-validation (5 or 10 outer folds) with 95% confidence intervals, family-grouped and site-grouped cross-validation with whole families or sites held out, temporal hold-out, PCA baselines and 1,000-permutation tests add to it. Regression is scored with R², adjusted R², MAE and RMSE. Classification is scored with AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, accuracy, precision, recall and F1, with calibration (expected calibration error, Brier score, Platt and isotonic recalibration) and decision curves.

docs.title: Subgroups and fairness
docs.text: Performance is reported by child sex, parent sex and education, SES, adverse life events, race/ethnicity and religion, with a partial-correlation check for demographic confounds (stages stratified and fairness).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Many predictors and outcomes share raters and measurement methods, and shared rater and method variance remain central to interpretation. The predictive advantage of subjective and informant ratings is partly inseparable from shared rater variance, shared method variance, prior symptom stability and construct covariance.

The circularity protocol reduces direct leakage but does not eliminate all rater, method, or ambiguous latent construct covariance.

Associations are observational. Feature importance is exploratory and descriptive, and directionality cannot be inferred from it.

Later waves overlap the COVID-19 pandemic, so developmental effects cannot be fully separated from pandemic-period perturbations.

Several domains (neuroimaging, experimental tasks, Fitbit) were collected only in adolescents, so the adolescent and parent analyses are not fully symmetric.

All models were developed and evaluated within ABCD. How they generalize to other cohorts is untested.

docs.title: Ethical considerations
docs.text: The models and their outputs must not be used to make decisions about individuals. Participant privacy is protected by the Data Use Certification and by the safeguards in Data access and governance.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: The repository ships a fully simulated panel (data/simulated/) with the same columns and five-wave structure as the analysis file. Its columns are drawn independently, so nothing in it is predictable. bpsp example-panel resamples it and plants a known signal at wave T2 in four predictors (bpsp.simulation), which gives the demo a correct answer to recover.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
bpsp example-panel outputs/example_panel.csv
bpsp run configs/demo.yaml

This runs setup (registry, circularity exclusions, preprocessing, model configuration) and the stages listed in the config, writing tables, figures, run.log and the resolved configuration to outputs/demo/. In run.log, the ensemble's held-out R² for internal_D_p should be about 0.42, and the four planted predictors (Change in Unliked, Blames Others, Stubborn, Disagreeable) should head "Top Features by Weighted Consensus".

Weighted consensus feature importance from the quickstart notebook, on a simulated panel in which four predictors carry the signal. The pipeline ranks them first. Simulated data, not a result of the article.

Two warnings near the start are expected with the simulated panel. It lacks 24 variables that the registry lists, mostly parent self-report items ("columns were not found in the dataset and have been dropped"), and some of its columns are more than 70% missing at T2, so they are dropped (the message says "Dropped columns at t = 2 due to entirely missing data"). The adjusted R² column of the metrics table is empty in the demo, because the demo has fewer test rows than predictors (see Methods in brief).

Run other stages, or override the output directory:

bpsp run configs/demo.yaml --stages main,networks,base_learners --output-dir outputs/try2
bpsp stages                     # list every stage
bpsp init-config my_run.yaml    # a config file with every setting at its published default

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
from bpsp import Pipeline, PipelineConfig, ctx

cfg = PipelineConfig.from_yaml("configs/demo.yaml")
cfg.main.target_options = "internal_D_p"
cfg.main.split = "across_categories"
cfg.main.tp_option = "2"

pipe = Pipeline(cfg)
pipe.run(["main", "base_learners"])

ctx.metrics_dict_full  # held-out metrics per base learner and the ensemble
ctx.consensus_df  # consensus feature importance
ctx.X_train.shape  # the exact training matrix used
pipe.timings  # seconds per stage

Stages can also be run one at a time, which mirrors running notebook cells:

pipe = Pipeline(cfg)
pipe.setup()
pipe.run_stage("main")
pipe.run_stage("nested_cv")

docs.title: Runtime on real data
docs.text: Within-category single-target runs vary with the data available at each wave. An across-category single-target run (~420 features, N ≈ 10,000) took about 15 to 45 minutes on an A100. The validation stages from nested_cv to temporal_gradient took 3 to 30 hours for one target, mostly depending on the number of permutations and folds.

docs.text: A run is setup followed by any sequence of stages. Each stage is one module in src/bpsp/ and corresponds to one cell of the published notebook (paper/ABCDMLPipeline_v1.0.0.ipynb). docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Suite Command What it checks Time Unit pytest -m "not integration and not slow" run context, configuration and its validation, CLI, logging, stage registry, variable registry and circularity exclusions, leakage guards, the simulated example panel, the data guard, and that the documented v2 edits match the published notebook seconds Integration pytest -m integration complete runs on simulated data (regression and classification), the CLI, and the known-answer checks below about 2 minutes Equivalence pytest -m slow the package gives the same results as the published notebook (paper/) on the same simulated panel about 45 minutes

CI runs these checks on every pull request and every push to main:

  • ruff, the data guard, and actionlint on the workflow files
  • mypy on the hand-written modules
  • the unit tests on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13, with a coverage report
  • the integration tests and a CLI demo
  • the quickstart notebook, a wheel build and the documentation build

The equivalence workflow runs weekly and on demand, in the pinned environment of requirements-lock.txt. Times are for a two-core machine.

Unit-test coverage of the hand-written modules (pipeline, configuration, run context, CLI, logging, simulation) is 94%. The stage modules are exercised by the integration and equivalence tests instead.

docs.title: Leakage guards
docs.text:
tests/test_leakage_guards.py, on the simulated panel, checks that:

  • the target and every variable on its circularity-exclusion list are absent from the predictors
  • scaling statistics come from training rows only, and training and test rows are disjoint (70/30 split)
  • the meta-learner is fitted on out-of-fold base-learner predictions, never on predictions for rows a base learner was trained on
  • family-grouped cross-validation keeps all members of a family in the same fold
  • permutation p-values use the Phipson-Smyth correction, (b + 1) / (m + 1), so they are never zero

docs.title: Known answers
docs.text: On a panel with a signal planted in four predictors (bpsp.simulation), those four rank first in the consensus importance and the ensemble's held-out R² is above 0.25 (tests/test_known_answer.py). On the shipped panel, whose columns are independent, the held-out R² stays below 0.1 (tests/test_integration.py).

docs.title: Registry integrity
docs.text: Outcome lists do not overlap, feature pools are not empty, and a session does not change the published variable registry (tests/test_registry_integrity.py).

docs.title: Equivalence with v1.0.0
docs.text: The frozen notebook runs cell by cell in an IPython shell and the package stage by stage, on the same simulated panel. After every step the two runs are compared on fingerprints of every shared result (splits, metrics, archives, validation tables), their printed output and every file they write. Four plans in tests/regression/plans/ cover every stage between them: a regression run with most validation stages, a second regression run with the remaining validation stages and diagnostics, a classification batch, and a within-category run with the objective/subjective gradient. The results are in Equivalence.

docs.title: What the tests do not show
docs.text:
They do not reproduce the article's findings. Every test uses simulated data. The scientific results depend on ABCD data, which cannot be used in CI, and were produced with v1.0.0 (paper/).

They do not show that v1.0.0 itself is right. The equivalence tests show that v2.0.0 does what v1.0.0 does, including its known issues, not that every analysis choice is correct.

They do not cover full scale. The tests use small panels (300 to 1,200 simulated participants) and small models, so runtime, memory use and TabPFN on a GPU at the scale of the published analyses are not tested.

Apart from the guards above, the validation stages (calibration, fairness, ablation and others) are checked for running end to end and for matching v1.0.0, not against independently computed reference values.
